claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has a single-phase, homogeneous solid-solution microstructure in the proposed starting state.
The low hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi are primarily caused by its homogeneous solid-solution state.
The homogeneous matrix promotes facile dislocation motion on multiple slip systems.
The solid solution has a low intrinsic lattice resistance to dislocation motion, such as a low Peierls barrier.
The pristine CoCrFeNiTi microstructure lacks effective precipitate or segregated grain-boundary obstacles.
A minor boron addition to CoCrFeNiTi will induce intergranular or intragranular precipitates.
Boron-induced grain-boundary precipitates impede dislocation motion.
Dislocation glide in the unmodified alloy occurs on multiple {110} or similar slip systems.
Easy glide produces distributed, small slip events.
Distributed small slip events lead to limited dislocation pile-up and limited work hardening.
Intergranular nanoprecipitates generated by the addition will arrest or pin dislocations.
The boron-added alloy will have higher grain-boundary hardness than the unmodified alloy.
The boron-added alloy will have higher overall yield strength than the unmodified alloy.
Dislocation pinning will be observable near precipitates in the boron-added alloy.
The unmodified alloy will show widespread, relatively unconstrained slip together with low hardness and yield strength.
Room-temperature loading at moderate strain rates and strains will not induce a phase transformation.
The controlled comparison uses otherwise identically tested unmodified and boron-added CoCrFeNiTi samples.
A statistically insignificant change in hardness, yield strength, or dislocation behavior is proposed as falsification of the obstacle-controlled strengthening hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention is intended to create secondary precipitates, whereas the conditions and boundary broadly require preservation of a simple solid-solution state and no secondary-phase formation. This can only be reconciled if the no-transformation boundary is explicitly limited to deformation-induced changes after precipitates have already formed.
